phase1.intro:
Three ways to repeat code, and each answers a slightly different question.

Which loop do you want to meet first?

topics.buttonText: When should I reach for a for loop?
dialogue: `for` is your go-to when you already know how many times you're repeating — the whole `for (initialization; condition; increment)` header is really just "start here, keep going while this is true, do this after every lap."

stickyNote.flavor: 🔁 use it when you know the lap count
stickyNote.definition: for (init; condition; increment) — runs init once, repeats while condition is true, runs increment after each iteration.

topics.buttonText: What's the difference between while and do-while?
dialogue: `while` is for when you don't know the count up front, just the condition that should keep things going — like adding numbers until some running total passes a threshold.

`do-while` is the one guaranteed to run at least once, [[key:because it checks its condition AFTER the loop body, not before]] — useful any time you need something to happen at least one time no matter what, like showing a menu before asking whether to repeat it.

stickyNote.definition: while checks its condition before each pass. do-while checks after — guaranteeing the loop body runs at least once.

topics.buttonText: What do break and continue actually do?
dialogue: Inside any loop, `break` exits the whole loop immediately, and `continue` just skips the rest of THIS lap and jumps to the next one.
[[warn:while (true) with no break anywhere inside is an infinite loop]] — sometimes intentional, usually not.

stickyNote.flavor: ⛔ break leaves, continue just skips ahead
stickyNote.definition: break exits the loop entirely. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one.

phase1.openingDialogue: for, while, and do-while all repeat code — the question is just whether you know the count, the condition, or need it to run at least once. 🔂

phase2.errorMessage:
(Program runs forever! No error message — but the code never stops.)

Sum: 1
Sum: 2
Sum: 3
Sum: 4
Sum: 5
Sum: 6
Sum: 7
... infinite ...
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:This loop never ends, because counter never changes]] — `counter <= 5` starts true and just stays true forever, since nothing inside the loop body ever touches `counter`.

[[key:Every loop needs a clear path toward its condition eventually becoming false]] — here that means adding `counter++` somewhere inside the loop body, so `counter` eventually climbs past 5 and the loop actually ends.

A good habit whenever you write a loop: look at the condition, then ask yourself "what inside this loop is actually changing to make that condition eventually false?" If the answer is nothing, you've found your bug before running it even once.

phase3.openingDialogue: Time to loop — don't get caught in an infinite one! 🔄

mcq.question:
Which loop is guaranteed to run its body at least once, no matter the condition?

A) for
B) while
C) do-while
D) None — all loops can run zero times

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a program that:
1. Uses a for loop to print numbers 10 down to 1
2. Uses a while loop to add numbers 1 to 100 and print the sum (5050)

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: the for-each loop (`for (int num : numbers)`) isn't actually a separate feature under the hood — for arrays, the compiler quietly rewrites it into a regular indexed for loop, and for collections, it rewrites it to use an Iterator instead. It's what's sometimes called "syntactic sugar" — a nicer way to write something the language could already do.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more loop-shaped thought before you go~
